title: Nathan Fielder’s movie on Elizabeth Holmes absolutely lives up to the hype
content: About a third of the way through “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes , we watch the disgraced Theranos founder and convicted fraudster pose for the camera — more than 200 of them, to be exact. In the days before she reported to federal prison in 2023, Holmes had her likeness captured and scanned so she can be reproduced via video, hologram and artificial intelligence while she’s locked up. It’s partly a business decision — she and partner William “Billy” Evans, with whom she shares two children, are launching a new healthcare startup (which they refer to as Theranos 2.0), and it might be useful to have access to a version of Holmes that can be programmed, say, to give pitches. And yet, we see Holmes crying. She’s been hurt before by putting her image too far out into the public. “I have a weird history with being on camera,” she says, sobbing. Thanks to “You Can See Everything,” that history is only getting weirder. The pre-release buzz around this new movie, which was made in secret and revealed via a surprise trailer that dropped last month, has been near deafening. Some of the critics who had been privy to its secrets have boldly declared it “the movie of the year” or wondered whether it might even become the first documentary to receive an Oscar nomination for best picture. With the film opening in theaters across the US on Friday, audiences now have their turn to see what all the fuss is about. Fielder’s movie is a wholly unique and revolutionary one. Thanks to the unparalleled access to Holmes and her family in the days before her incarceration (at one point we even see Evans showering nude), as well as some truly jaw-dropping creative decisions later in the movie, the film is gripping and shocking. It is a bold, perhaps impossible, quest for truth about someone whom Fielder compares to a magician. At one point, he wonders if she may just be the most manipulative person who has ever lived. Rarely, if ever, has a documentarian and subject been so perfectly matched. Through his shows “Nathan for You” and “The Rehearsal,” Fielder has established himself as someone pathologically obsessed with elaborate schemes, awkwardness, meta narratives and things that are not what they first appear. In these programs, Fielder plays both the straight man and the chaos agent, often appearing like an alien in human disguise sent to study our most inexplicable behavior, even if it means meddling in things himself. If Fielder is again playing a version of himself here, Holmes seems to be offering near infinite versions of herself up for examination, like a set of unblinking reflections in a hall of funhouse mirrors. As the movie progresses, Fielder and the audience must question whether and how they’re being deceived. Is Holmes just weird, as Evans, her partner, insists? A victim of the men in her life, as her father seems to believe? Someone who may be on the spectrum and incapable of understanding how others perceive her words, as a revelatory sequence involving Holmes’ reaction to the Abbott and Costello “Who’s On First” sketch seems to suggest? Or is she just a compulsive liar who has somehow managed to delude even herself? “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true. So what is the reality?” Holmes says in the movie. It’s a question that hovers over the entire production and one that isn’t easily answered. Co-directed by Fielder and Oppenheim, the latter of whom released “ Primetime ” also under the A24 banner last month, “You Can See Everything” is somehow visually gorgeous and yet profoundly ugly — almost intentionally so. Much of it is filmed in extreme close-up, replete with zits, wrinkles and sweat on Fielder and Holmes, as if we’re studying them under a microscope. As befitting Fielder’s style for leaning into artifice, we often see the crew and their boom mics, as they work to create something that ultimately mixes reality and recreation, fact and fiction. A surprise person appears halfway through the movie — one being kept a closely guarded secret from audiences and which we won’t spoil here — but whose presence transforms it entirely, emerging as both co-documentarian and co-subject. “We’re working in Fiction Land,” this person astutely observes at one point. That feels like an understatement. Fielder is a refreshingly candid guide through this strange land. He’s open about his insecurities as to why Holmes wanted him to capture her — does his lack of scientific understanding mean he’ll be an easy mark? — and the movie offers the case that he may have grown too close to or fond of his subject. When one person remarks that Holmes may be a victim of Stockholm Syndrome under Evans, viewers can only wonder if the same can be said for Fielder and Holmes. When Holmes does eventually report to federal prison in Texas, she does so after Fielder injects his trademark cringe into her last moments of freedom, suggesting he leave Holmes and Evans alone so they can have sex — then asking how it was — and offering her a gag gift in front of her parents of hair dye and sunglasses so that she can go on the run. Then, as she prepares to get into the car to leave Fielder, they embrace and stare awkwardly at one another until we finally hear the words, “You’ve got this.” But it’s not Fielder who says this to Holmes in a bid to lift her spirits. It’s she who is encouraging him , as if she knows the Herculean task he has ahead of him in trying to make sense of her. It’s a stunning reversal of roles to capture on camera, but also feels entirely appropriate for a film that has rewritten the rules of documentaries as we know them.

title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as deadly boredom sets in on The Celebrity Traitors
content:
For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom.
The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn.
Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight.
The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious.
If one of the faithful succumbs to the traitors' soporific tactics and yawns as well, they will be put to sleep for good.
We must wait until next Thursday to find out who, if anyone, is murdered in plain sight. That was what passed as a nail-biting cliffhanger this week.
There was, thankfully, some more animated action elsewhere in Friday's episode.
After Thursday saw King Kenny recruited by the traitors - that episode ending with his deliciously evil laugh - the YouTuber and former aspiring boxer brought fresh and fiendish energy to the turret.
"This threesome's going to be different," mama traitor Maya Jama predicted. "There's a new vibrance."
James Acaster, her reluctant fellow traitor, was also happy with their choice of ally.
"As predicted, Kenny's taken to this like a duck to water," the comedian said, visibly relieved. "He's the opposite of me. So relaxed. He's a natural born traitor."
Kenny is relishing the role, barely able to disguise his pleasure as Miranda Hart confided to him over breakfast that "you're my main faithful".
The self-declared modern-day Miss Marple warned Kenny to be on the lookout for anyone acting differently, reasoning that "if you're suddenly a traitor, you're going to be a bit on high alert".
"I agree," was his straight-faced reply.
In the show's diary room, he said: "The first taste of being on the other side - it does feel good, because you have the power.
"I'm good at staying calm because as a boxer you have to have a poker face. You can't let the other people know that you're intimidated."
However, he later admitted: "On the outside I look calm, cool, collected, but on the inside I'm incredibly nervous."
Meanwhile, all eyes were on a different player as the traitors' possible new recruit.
The previous day, Joe Lycett had loudly declared that he longed for a ticket to the turret - and even though it would have been, as he later protested, too obvious for the traitors to grant him his wish, it was enough to arouse suspicion.
Acaster observed: "I feel like today is one of those days where maybe we [traitors] don't even have to do anything. You have no idea of the gift that I've been given."

title: I hope Marvel fans accept my Scottish accent, says new star Ruaridh Mollica
content:
Scottish actor Ruaridh Mollica has said he hopes fans will accept his accent as he stars in the latest addition to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU).
The 27-year-old plays the speedster Tommy Maximoff in the new Disney+ miniseries VisionQuest, which is based on the superhero comic book character Vision.
Tommy is an 18-year-old orphan who is newly out of the foster care system in London but has memories of his mother and father - Avengers Wanda Maximoff and Vision.
Mollica told The Saturday Show on BBC Radio Scotland that speaking in his own accent helped him give the character a fuller personality.
"I want the fans to like what I have done with the character and accept that I have a Scottish accent," he said.
"It threw a lot of people off at the start, but having my own accent meant I could put my own spin on the character."
The eight-episode series has been described as the conclusion of a trilogy that also includes WandaVision and Agatha All Along.
Its cast includes Marvel veteran Paul Bettany, award-winning actor James Spader and British performer Joe Locke, who Mollica made his London West End debut with.
When Mollica was added to the lineup in October 2025, he described it as "the best day of my life".
"I submitted the self tape into the abyss thinking I'm never going to get the role, but after a five-month audition process I was on the plane to New York to do a screen test with Paul Bettany and Terry Matalas, who created the series," he said.
"My manager in America phoned me and goes, 'your life is about to change, kid,' and I just cried.
"I bawled my eyes out, sat on a wall and it started raining in a prophetic fallacy kind of way."
Mollica, who was born in Italy to a Scottish mother and an Italian father but grew up in Edinburgh, worked on-and-off as an actor in his teenage years and early 20s.
He made his television debut aged 12 in an episode of the BBC One series Case Histories and made his film debut as a background dancer in the Sunshine on Leith adaptation.
The 27-year-old went on to appear in the drama Stonemouth, an adaptation of the novel by Scottish author Iain Banks, and the romance film Tell It to the Bees.
During his final year at university, he played a lead role the short film Too Rough, which won a Scottish Bafta.
The Scot graduated with a Bachelor of Science in computer science from Heriot-Watt University in 2021.
"After my degree, I thought about doing a masters degree, but acting stole my heart," Mollica said.
"I still cannot believe it."
The 27-year-old said when he was first cast in the role he put a lot of pressure on himself and suffered from imposter syndrome.
